Subject: Capacity headroom / top-up modeling question

Hi Nikhil,

Thanks again for the product walkthrough last week. We're working through sizing for our first Dedicated pool and hit a few follow-ups on the top-up (burst) model that I'd like to confirm before we finalize numbers with procurement. Attached is our capacity workbook showing expected daily throughput and a couple of traffic spikes during monthly batch jobs (acme_capacity_workbook.xlsx).

Short list of clarifying questions:
- How is "capacity headroom" priced when we set a small reserved commit but expect short, sharp spikes? Is billing per vGPU-hour consumed during bursts, or do you prorate smaller increments?
- What is the default cooldown window after a burst before the pool scales down? Can that cooldown be shortened for high-priority workloads? Any pricing delta?
- Do burst requests count against throughput guarantees or are guarantees measured only against the reserved baseline?
- For planned events (monthly ingest), can we temporarily increase our headroom without paying peak surge rates (e.g., scheduled exception)? If so, what lead time and contract language is typical?

We'd like a short written example (numbers) we can show procurement. Can you share a quick model and any attachable pricing sheet?

Thanks,
Sarah Johnson
Head of Platform Operations
Acme Analytics

Attachment: acme_capacity_workbook.xlsx (spreadsheet, 78 KB)

From: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Capacity headroom / top-up modeling question

Hi Sarah — great to see the workbook, thanks for sending. Quick answers up front, then a short illustrative model and next steps. 

Summary answers:
- Billing increments: bursts are billed per minute of vGPU-equivalent consumption with a 5-minute minimum increment by default. We can offer 1-minute billing for latency-sensitive pools at an incremental premium.
- Cooldown: default cooldown is 10 minutes (time from last active request to scale-down). Shortening to 2-3 minutes is possible for high-priority pools with a +20% surge-rate premium.
- Guarantees: throughput SLAs (tokens/sec per reserved pool) apply to the reserved commit. Bursts are best-effort capacity beyond reserved baseline; we provide percentile-based reporting (95th/99th) for combined traffic but SLA crediting only applies to the committed baseline unless you purchase a managed surge SLA add-on.
- Scheduled exceptions: yes — we support scheduled headroom reservations (temporary top-up commitments) with a lower per-unit rate than on-demand surge. Typical lead time is 5 business days for capacity planning; legal addendum can specify scheduled window(s) to avoid peak surge pricing.

Illustrative model (using numbers from your workbook):
- Reserved commit: 8 vGPU-equivalents (baseline) at $X,XXX/mo (example).
- Typical day usage: baseline covers 92% of minutes.
- On-demand surge: additional vGPU-minutes billed at $0.60 per vGPU-minute (billed in 5-minute increments).
- 1-month pilot offer: 15% discount on surge rate for the first 90 days if you sign a 12-month reserved commit.
- Cooldown variants: default 10-minute cooldown (no premium); 2-minute cooldown option at +20% to the surge rate; scheduled headroom (prebooked window) at surge rate minus 25% (requires 5 business days notice).

I've attached a concise pricing sheet (redwood_dedicated_topup_pricing_v2.pdf) and a worked example export for one of your spike days.

Next steps: do you want a short SOW (pilot terms + pricing tables) and a procurement-ready line-item summary? We can also model a capped monthly top-up spend if you prefer a maximum monthly exposure.

Best,

From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>

Date: Tue, 16 Mar 2027 09:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Internal: Capacity headroom — pricing levers and exceptions

Looping in a couple of internal questions / suggestions before we send a procurement-ready doc to Acme: 

- For high-priority pools (finance/real-time pipelines) I support offering the 2-minute cooldown option but only if we attach a throughput cap per pool and a 20% premium. That reduces churn and makes billing predictable.
- Consider a hard monthly cap option: customer prepays a top-up bucket at a discounted rate (e.g., 10% off on-demand) that can be consumed at 1-minute granularity. Once the bucket is exhausted, fall back to on-demand surge rate. This helps procurement lock exposure.
- Legal: Ben, can we add a clause for "scheduled exemptions" where prebooked windows are eligible for pre-negotiated pricing (must be requested >5 business days)? Any concerns with capacity guarantees when many customers request overlapping windows?
- Operations: do we need to gate the scheduled exception by regional capacity (us-west availability zone)? If yes, let's capture that in the SOW as potential fallback behavior.

If everyone agrees, I'll draft a two-page SOW and a single-page price summary for procurement.

— Monica
Monica Patel
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

Thanks — quick procurement/finance notes: 

- Billing granularity: we can agree to 1-minute billing for select customers but need a short-term commitment (3 months minimum) for billing systems. Otherwise default 5-minute increments.
- Prepaid top-up bucket: finance is fine with a prepay bucket model. Suggested mechanics: customer prepays for N vGPU-hours at discounted rate; we track consumption; once exhausted, automatic fallthrough to on-demand surge with alerting. We should include an option for rollover (unused minutes roll to next month) or no-rollover per customer preference.
- Minimum charge for surge events: recommend a 15-minute minimum invoice increment for corporate customers to simplify reconciliation (we already do 5-minute usage accounting internally). This prevents micro-invoices while still supporting fine-grained autoscaling.
- DocuSign SOW: I'll prepare a proc-friendly SOW with those options and include DocuSign workflow. Link for draft SOW: https://www.docusign.com/123456789/sow-acme-dedicated
